subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Shape Faces: Craft, Name, and Place

tasks_in_class.description: Use old boxes (cubes and cuboids) and bottles (cylinders) to do craft work. Draw faces on them. What did you draw on their faces?
Jaya's rocket: identify shapes used, count each type; answer which shape is between red and yellow cuboid, on top of orange cylinder, under pink cone.

time_bands.activity: Children handle real boxes and bottles brought to class. Each child selects one object, feels its surface, and decides where to draw a face on it. Let us Do, p.9 ("Use old boxes and bottles to do craft work....") guides the making. Pairs share what they drew and name the object's solid shape — cube, cuboid, cylinder, or cone.

Introduce face, edge, and corner using a labelled cube held up for the class. Children point to each feature on their own object and name it aloud. The teacher displays or sketches the labelled diagram from the chapter.

Children work on Let us Do, p.9 ("Jaya's rocket: identify shapes used, count each type....") as a whole-class discussion. The teacher reads each positional question aloud — between, on top of, under — and children respond by pointing to or naming the relevant shape, practising spatial vocabulary alongside shape names.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who confuse the cone with the cylinder can be guided to run a finger along the base edges: the cylinder has two circular edges while the cone tapers to a point. The positional questions — between, on top, under — are as important as the shape names, so give each position question its own brief pause. A common slip at this stage is calling any box a 'cube'; encourage children to check whether all faces look the same size before using that name.
materials: Chapter illustration of Jaya's rocket (textbook p.9)

tasks_in_class.description: Count and fill: how many red cylinders, yellow cones, grey cuboids, blue cubes in Devika's toy engine.
What shapes are used in these toys? (dog, lollipop, cat, block-set toy images)
Collect objects to make a house; name shapes, talk about faces and edges (straight/curved); describe arrangement; what part of shapes can you see from a distance?

time_bands.activity: Children open to Let us Do, p.10 ("Count and fill: how many red cylinders, yellow cones, grey cuboids, blue cubes...."). Each child counts independently, then the class shares answers. The teacher asks how children distinguished a cube from a cuboid in the engine, drawing out the special-type relationship: a cube is a special cuboid where all faces are the same size.

Let us Discuss, p.10 ("What shapes are used in these toys?") is worked as a class. The teacher points to the dog, lollipop, cat, and block-set images in turn; children name the shapes they see and justify — 'the lollipop stick is a cylinder because it has two flat circular faces and curved sides.' The teacher records shape names on the board as children offer them.

Small groups use collected objects (boxes, cylinders, cones) to assemble a house or tower following Let us Discuss, p.10 ("Collect objects to make a house; name shapes, talk about faces and edges...."). Each group names the shapes used, describes one face as flat or curved, and shares one observation about how shapes look from across the room. The teacher circulates and prompts: 'Which part of this shape can you see from far away?'

periods.teacher_notes: Children often overlook that a cube is a special cuboid; draw out this point explicitly when children report the engine count. For the toy-discussion task, encourage children to explain their reasoning — 'I said cone because it has a point at the top' — rather than just naming. A frequent error in the building task is describing all faces as flat; guide children to roll a cylinder on the desk to feel and name its curved surface.
materials: Collected solid objects (boxes, bottles, cone-shaped items)
Chalkboard or whiteboard for recording shape names

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Play (Construct and Describe), p.11
tasks_in_class.description: In groups: one student selects 3 shapes, assembles them, describes the sequence; others build the same without seeing the original. Take turns.
Find classroom objects shaped like cylinder/sphere/cube/cuboid/cone; fill table; name shape found most and least; name objects made of more than one shape.

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly recaps property vocabulary — flat face, curved face, straight edge, curved edge — by holding up a cylinder and asking children to call out the property as the teacher points to each surface. This anchors the language children will need during the game.

Groups play Let us Play (Construct and Describe), p.11 ("In groups: one student selects 3 shapes, assembles them, describes the sequence...."). The describer may only use shape names and position words (on, under, next to); no pointing. After each round the group checks whether the built arrangement matches. Roles rotate so every child has a turn describing.

Children carry out Let us Do Q1, p.11 ("Find classroom objects shaped like cylinder/sphere/cube/cuboid/cone; fill table....") individually, moving quietly around the room to find and record one example per shape. Pairs then compare tables, agree on the shape found most and least, and name one object made of more than one shape. A brief whole-class share closes the hunt.

periods.teacher_notes: Children playing the Construct and Describe game sometimes gesture or point; insist on words only so that spatial language — on top of, to the left of, next to — gets genuine exercise. In the classroom hunt, children may struggle to find a sphere; prompt them to think of balls or round fruit. A common error is listing only one property when describing a shape; encourage children to mention both face type and edge type.
materials: Collected solid objects or shape models (cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere)
Tally or fill-in table sheet (or notebook)

periods.activity_title: Sort by Properties, Reason with Rules

tasks_in_class.description: Circle the cubes; tick the cones; cross the cylinders; draw a box around the cuboids (from a mixed group of shape images).
Name shapes: with no edges; with only flat faces; with only curved faces; with both straight and curved edges; with both flat and curved faces.

time_bands.activity: Children work individually on Let us Do Q2, p.12 ("Circle the cubes; tick the cones; cross the cylinders; draw a box around the cuboids...."). The teacher circulates, pausing to ask a child who has circled an image: 'How did you know that is a cube and not a cuboid?' After independent work, answers are checked whole-class with the teacher asking for justification before confirming.

Let us Do Q3, p.12 ("Name shapes: with no edges; with only flat faces; with only curved faces....") is worked as a class discussion. The teacher writes each property prompt on the board; children hold up a matching solid object or name it. After each property is resolved the teacher asks: 'Can we name another shape that also fits this rule?' Building a class-compiled list on the board reinforces how properties distinguish shapes.

periods.teacher_notes: Children working on the classification task frequently mark a cone as having 'only curved faces' because they see the curved side; draw attention to the flat circular base to correct this. For the property-reasoning task, some children may say 'sphere' for 'only flat faces' — hold up a sphere and ask them to find a flat part, guiding them to discover it has none. Pairing children who finish early to quiz each other using property clues deepens the reasoning further.
materials: Solid objects or shape models for reference during discussion

tasks_in_class.description: Which shapes can you build? Make shapes using clay and sticks (cube-skeleton and octahedron-skeleton shown as examples).
Try to make the given shapes using cubes (two example cube-block configurations shown).
In how many different ways can you join 3 cubes? What shape do you get if you join a cube and a cuboid? How many cubes make the given shape?

time_bands.activity: Children follow Let us Do Q4, p.13 ("Make shapes using clay and sticks...."), using clay balls as joints and sticks as edges to build a cube-skeleton. The teacher counts edges and corners with the class as they build. Children then attempt any other skeleton shape they can invent, naming it if they can.

Each child or pair uses small cubes (wooden blocks or sugar-cube-sized objects) for Let us Do Q5, p.13 ("Try to make the given shapes using cubes...."). They replicate the two configurations shown in the book, then try one arrangement of their own and describe it to a neighbour.

Children explore Let us Do Q9, p.15 ("In how many different ways can you join 3 cubes?...") in pairs, physically arranging three cubes and recording or sketching each distinct arrangement. The teacher collects results on the board, asking: 'Is this arrangement really different from that one, or the same shape turned around?' This surfaces the idea of spatial equivalence in an informal way.

periods.teacher_notes: Children building clay skeletons sometimes add too many sticks, losing track of the edges of a cube; counting aloud — twelve edges, eight corners — before starting helps. For the three-cube joining task, the key challenge is deciding whether a rotated version counts as a different arrangement; let children debate this rather than resolving it prematurely, as the reasoning process is the learning. Keep clay pieces small so building stays quick and tactile.
materials: Small unit cubes (wooden blocks, sugar cubes, or interlocking cubes)
Textbook open to p.13 and p.15

periods.activity_title: Compare Shapes, Sequence a Build, Explore Dice

tasks_in_class.description: In what ways are these shapes (cylinder, cube, cuboid, cone, sphere) the same? In what ways are they different?
Look at a die (faces 1–6). What number is on the face opposite 1? Opposite 2? Opposite 3? What pattern do you notice?
In what order is this model built? (table-like model with cuboid base, cylinder supports, and cone tops)

time_bands.activity: The class works on Let us Do Q6, p.14 ("In what ways are these shapes the same? In what ways are they different?"). The teacher draws a two-column table (same / different) on the board. Children suggest comparisons — 'a cylinder and a cuboid both have flat faces' — and the teacher records them. Pairs can first discuss in their own words before sharing.

Each group is given a die for Let us Do Q7, p.14 ("What number is on the face opposite 1? Opposite 2? Opposite 3?"). Children turn the die, record the opposite-face pairs, and then discuss: 'What do opposite faces always add up to?' The teacher guides towards noticing the sum-of-seven pattern without stating it first.

Let us Do Q8, p.14 ("In what order is this model built?") is tackled as a class. The teacher projects or holds up the book image of the table-like model; children suggest a building order and explain why — 'we need the cuboid base first or the cylinders have nothing to stand on.' The teacher asks children to justify each step before moving to the next.

periods.teacher_notes: Children comparing shapes often focus only on visual similarity rather than geometric properties; prompt 'What can you tell me about the faces?' to keep reasoning anchored to properties built earlier in the chapter. For the die task, some children will simply list the pairs without noticing the pattern; ask 'What do 1 and 6 add to? And 2 and 5?' to guide them toward the sum-of-seven observation. The sequencing task works best when children explain their reasoning step by step rather than jumping to a final order.
materials: Solid shape models (cylinder, cube, cuboid, cone, sphere)

periods.activity_title: Name Models, Build with Dice, Play the Shape Game

tasks_in_class.description: Name the shapes used in models (a)(b)(c)(d). Describe how the shapes are arranged.
Use six dice to make: (a) a cuboid (b) a tower (c) any other shape of your choice.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Play (Shape Board Game), p.12–13
tasks_in_class.description: Roll die, move counter to next picture matching number's shape (1=Cylinder, 2=Sphere, 3=Cone, 4=Cube, 5=Cuboid, 6=Move 2 forward). First to Finish wins.

time_bands.activity: Children study the four models in Let us Do Q10, p.15 ("Name the shapes used in models (a)(b)(c)(d). Describe how the shapes are arranged.") individually, then pairs share their descriptions. The teacher selects one model and asks: 'Which shape is at the base? What sits on top of it and why does that make sense?' This links to spatial reasoning developed through counting shapes in compound objects.

Groups of three use six dice for Let us Do Q11, p.15 ("Use six dice to make: a cuboid, a tower, any other shape of your choice."). Each group builds all three and then presents one to the class, naming what they made and how they arranged the dice. The teacher asks: 'Is the arrangement you made really a cuboid? How do you know?'

Children play Let us Play (Shape Board Game), p.12–13 ("Roll die, move counter to next picture matching number's shape....") in groups of three or four. Each time a child moves, they must say the shape name aloud before placing the counter. The teacher listens for correct shape identification and prompts quietly where a child hesitates.

periods.teacher_notes: Children describing the models in Q10 sometimes say 'the long one is on the bottom' rather than naming the shape; redirect by asking 'What solid shape is that long one — is it a cuboid, a cylinder, something else?' For the dice-building task, children may struggle to see that six dice packed two-by-three form a cuboid; asking them to count the flat rectangular faces of the final arrangement helps. The board game moves quickly, so insist on the rule that the shape name must be spoken aloud to keep recognition active rather than automatic.
materials: Textbook open to p.15 and p.12–13
Board game counters (buttons or small tokens)

periods.activity_title: Toy Joy Review: Name, Sort, Build, and Describe

tasks_in_class.description: Name shapes: with no edges; with only flat faces; with only curved faces; with both straight and curved edges; with both flat and curved faces.
Look at a die (faces 1–6). What number is on the face opposite 1? Opposite 2? Opposite 3? What pattern do you notice?

time_bands.activity: The teacher presents five solid objects — cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere — and asks children to sort them into two groups of their own choosing, naming the rule they used. Groups share their sorting rules; the class discusses whether multiple rules are valid, revisiting the language of flat faces, curved faces, edges, and corners established across the chapter.

Children revisit Let us Do Q3, p.12 ("Name shapes: with no edges; with only flat faces; with only curved faces....") as a class challenge. The teacher reads each property aloud and children hold up — or point to — the matching solid. The teacher then adds a challenge: 'Can you think of a real object from your toy collection that fits this rule?'

Each child selects any three solid objects and places them in an arrangement, then writes or says two sentences describing the arrangement using position words (on, under, next to, between) and at least one shape property. Pairs listen to each other's descriptions and see whether they can replicate the arrangement — drawing on the Construct and Describe communication task from classifying shapes by properties.

A quick whole-class revisit of Let us Do Q7, p.14 ("Look at a die: what number is opposite 1? Opposite 2? Opposite 3? What pattern do you notice?") closes the unit. The teacher holds up a die, children call out opposite-face sums, and the teacher asks: 'The cube is one of our four shapes — what do we know about its faces, edges, and corners?' tying the die investigation back to shape properties.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the three threads of the chapter — naming and handling shapes, classifying by geometric properties, and communicating spatial arrangements — so children see how the craft and play activities connect to the underlying ideas about faces, edges, and corners. Watch for children who can name shapes confidently but still describe them only by appearance ('it looks round') rather than by property; the sorting and property tasks here offer a final opportunity to anchor property language. The die investigation at the close links the sum-of-seven pattern back to the cube's six equal faces, connecting the pattern-discovery work to the shape-attribute vocabulary built throughout.
materials: One set of solid shapes (cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere) per group
Dice (one per pair for the closing activity)
Textbook open to p.12 and p.14

items.prompt: Priya has a box of old containers. She picks one up and notices it has two flat circular faces and one curved surface all the way around. Which shape has she picked?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the shape by counting its flat circular faces (two) and noting the continuous curved surface.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may be guessing by object familiarity rather than reading the property clues.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child recognises a curved surface but does not notice there are two flat circular faces — a cone has only one.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may be thinking of a common container shape but ignoring the circular (not rectangular) faces described.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child hold a real cylinder and count the flat faces by touch; stretch: ask them to name a second real object that is also a cylinder.

exercise.description: Use old boxes (cubes and cuboids) and bottles (cylinders) to do craft work. Draw faces on them. What did you draw on their faces?

items.prompt: Look at the five solid shapes: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere. Choose any two shapes and write one way they are the same and one way they are different. Use words like face, edge, or corner in your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Answers will vary. A valid example: A cube and a cuboid are the same because both have only flat faces. They are different because a cube has six equal square faces while a cuboid has rectangular faces of different sizes. Accept any pair with a property-based same and property-based different statement.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare two shapes by naming a shared property (face type, edge type) and a distinguishing property.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child hold one shape in each hand and describe what they feel before writing; stretch: ask them to find a third shape that shares the same property they identified.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Play (Construct and Describe), p.11
exercise.description: In groups: one student selects 3 shapes, assembles them, describes the sequence; others build the same without seeing the original. Take turns.

items.prompt: Rani walks around her classroom and writes down all the objects she finds that are shaped like a sphere. Which of the following is most likely on her list?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the object whose shape has only a curved surface and no flat faces or edges — the defining property of a sphere.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may associate round with cylinders because bottles are common round objects, missing that a sphere has no flat faces.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child may be naming a common classroom object without reading it against the sphere's properties.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may confuse the pointed tip of a cone-shaped hat with the roundness of a sphere.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child hold a ball and a bottle and compare surfaces by touch before answering; stretch: ask them to name one more sphere-shaped object from their daily life.

exercise.description: Find classroom objects shaped like cylinder/sphere/cube/cuboid/cone; fill table; name shape found most and least; name objects made of more than one shape.

items.prompt: Rajan uses clay and sticks to build a skeleton of a cube. How many sticks does he need for the edges, and how many clay balls does he need for the corners? Write your answer and explain how you counted.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rajan needs 12 sticks (one for each edge of the cube) and 8 clay balls (one for each corner). A cube has 12 edges and 8 corners.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the edges and corners of a cube: 12 edges and 8 corners.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child build the skeleton physically and count sticks and balls as they place them; stretch: ask them to predict how many sticks and balls a cuboid skeleton would need and check.

exercise.description: Which shapes can you build? Make shapes using clay and sticks (cube-skeleton and octahedron-skeleton shown as examples).

items.prompt: Meera joins 3 small cubes so that each cube touches at least one face of another. Which of the following describes a way she could NOT arrange them?

options.label: A
options.text: All three in a straight row

options.label: B
options.text: Two in a row and one on top of the middle cube

options.label: C
options.text: One cube floating in the air with no contact

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One cube floating in the air with no contact
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the joining rule: each cube must touch at least one face of another, so a floating cube with no contact is impossible.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may think only unusual arrangements are valid, not recognising the straight row as a correct joining.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may think stacking is not a valid joining; stacking means two faces are in contact.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may think the L-shape is not a joining arrangement; in an L-shape each cube touches another face.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child try all four options physically with three cubes, then identify which is impossible; stretch: ask them to find and draw a fourth distinct arrangement of three cubes.

exercise.description: In how many different ways can you join 3 cubes? What shape do you get if you join a cube and a cuboid? How many cubes make the given shape?

items.prompt: Kabir builds a model rocket. The pointy tip is a cone. The middle part is a cylinder. The flat launch stand is a cuboid. Write the name of the shape that is on top of the cylinder. Then write the name of the shape that is under the cylinder.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The cone is on top of the cylinder. The cuboid is under the cylinder.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use positional language — on top of, under — to describe where each named shape sits in the model.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to point to the tip, middle, and bottom of a real rocket sketch before writing; stretch: ask them to add one more shape to the model and describe its position using a new position word.

exercise.description: Jaya's rocket: identify shapes used, count each type; answer which shape is between red and yellow cuboid, on top of orange cylinder, under pink cone.

items.prompt: A toy lollipop is made of a sphere on top of a long thin cylinder. Which statement best explains why the stick part is called a cylinder?

options.label: A
options.text: It is long and narrow, so it must be a cylinder.

options.label: B
options.text: It has two flat circular faces and a curved surface all the way around.

options.label: C
options.text: It has four flat rectangular faces like a box.

options.label: D
options.text: It has a pointed tip at one end.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: It has two flat circular faces and a curved surface all the way around.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Justify a shape name by checking its defining properties — flat circular faces and a curved surface — not by appearance alone.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child is classifying by visual appearance (long and narrow) rather than by geometric properties.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child is confusing a cylinder with a cuboid, possibly because both can appear elongated.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child is confusing a cylinder with a cone, describing the cone's defining feature (pointed tip).

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child hold a pencil (cylinder) and count its faces before choosing; stretch: ask them to explain why the round sweet on top is a sphere and not a cylinder.

exercise.description: What shapes are used in these toys? (dog, lollipop, cat, block-set toy images)

items.prompt: Write the name of a solid shape that has BOTH flat faces AND curved faces. Explain what makes it different from a shape that has only flat faces.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A cylinder or a cone has both flat and curved faces. A cylinder has two flat circular faces and one curved surface; a cone has one flat circular face and one curved surface. A shape with only flat faces — like a cube or cuboid — has no curved part at all; every face is flat and you cannot roll it smoothly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Name a shape by identifying its mix of flat and curved faces, then contrast with an all-flat-face shape.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child handle a cylinder and a cube side by side, running a finger over each surface before writing; stretch: ask them to name the shape that has only curved faces and explain why it is different from both.

exercise.description: Name shapes: with no edges; with only flat faces; with only curved faces; with both straight and curved edges; with both flat and curved faces.

items.prompt: A cylinder and a cone each have a curved surface. Write one way they are the same and one way they are different.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Same: both have a curved surface. Different: a cylinder has two flat circular faces while a cone has only one flat circular face and comes to a point (no second flat face at the top).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare two shapes on a shared property (curved surface) and a distinguishing property (number of flat faces).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child hold both shapes and point to the curved part, then count the flat faces on each; stretch: ask them to name a third shape that also has a curved surface and say how it differs from the first two.

exercise.description: In what ways are these shapes (cylinder, cube, cuboid, cone, sphere) the same? In what ways are they different?

items.prompt: Look at a die. The face showing 4 is opposite the face showing 3. The face showing 1 is opposite the face showing 6. The face showing 2 is opposite the face showing 5. What pattern do you notice? Write it in your own words.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Every pair of opposite faces on a die adds up to 7. So 1+6=7, 2+5=7, and 3+4=7.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add each opposite-face pair and observe that every pair sums to 7.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child hold a real die, turn it to find each opposite pair, and write the addition before writing the pattern; stretch: ask them to check whether this pattern would still hold if the die had faces numbered 1 to 6 in a different arrangement, and explain their thinking.

exercise.description: Look at a die (faces 1–6). What number is on the face opposite 1? Opposite 2? Opposite 3? What pattern do you notice?

items.prompt: A toy train engine is made of 2 cylinders, 3 cuboids, 1 cube, and 2 cones. How many solid shapes are used in the engine altogether?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the counts of each shape type: 2 + 3 + 1 + 2 = 8.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw a tally mark for each shape type and then count all the marks; stretch: ask them to write a new sentence saying how many more cuboids there are than cubes.

exercise.description: Count and fill: how many red cylinders, yellow cones, grey cuboids, blue cubes in Devika's toy engine.

items.prompt: A teacher puts four shape images on the board and asks children to circle only the cubes. Arjun looks at one image that shows a shape with six equal square faces. Should he circle it?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because it has six equal square faces, which means it is a cube.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because cubes and cuboids look the same.

options.label: C
options.text: No, because a cube has curved faces.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, because all boxes are cubes.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, because it has six equal square faces, which means it is a cube.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the defining property of a cube — six equal square faces — to confirm the identification.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child confuses cube and cuboid because both are box-shaped; they have not used the equal-faces property to distinguish them.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child has mis-remembered the cube's properties, possibly confusing it with a sphere or cylinder.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child correctly identifies the shape but for an incorrect reason — not all boxes are cubes, only those with six equal square faces.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child hold a cube and a cuboid side by side, counting and comparing faces before deciding; stretch: ask them to explain why a cereal box would NOT be circled even though it is also a box.

exercise.description: Circle the cubes; tick the cones; cross the cylinders; draw a box around the cuboids (from a mixed group of shape images).

items.prompt: In the shape board game, a player rolls the die and gets a 3. Which shape should the player move their counter to next?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the board game rule: 3 maps to Cone (1=Cylinder, 2=Sphere, 3=Cone, 4=Cube, 5=Cuboid).

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child maps 3 to Cylinder, possibly recalling 1=Cylinder but mis-shifting the number.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child maps 3 to Cube, confusing the number with the shape assigned to 4.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child maps 3 to Cuboid, confusing it with the number assigned to 5.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child write the number-to-shape key on a slip of paper and use it to look up the answer; stretch: ask them to say which shape a roll of 5 would send them to and explain how they know.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Play (Shape Board Game), p.12–13
exercise.description: Roll die, move counter to next picture matching number's shape (1=Cylinder, 2=Sphere, 3=Cone, 4=Cube, 5=Cuboid, 6=Move 2 forward). First to Finish wins.
